name: Tier default by the tier's own public metric
purpose: The default for each of the four tiers (fast, balanced, quality, best) is the cheapest and fastest arm that is at least as good as the tier's held default on public evaluations, by metric-tier-fast, -balanced, -quality and -best; best is capability only.
record: Per tier: the arms' public evaluation rows (tier_public_scores.csv), list prices (tier_prices.csv), the tier's minimums and weights (tier_metrics.csv), the score breakdown, and which arm the chooser picks and why. The hub's own measurements do not decide the model of a tier: which tier a call role uses is decided by the role-tier metric (metric-role-tier) over the same public rows, and passing work per cost (metric-tier-passing-work-per-cost) stays as the function select over measured arms.
disadvantages: A changed price, a new model or a leaderboard revision moves the ranking unseen until the rows are refreshed (45 days); the anchors are the held defaults, so a tier moves up only by a recorded change to its anchor; the public evaluations are an aggregator's, not the hub's own tasks.
cascading_conditionals: idea [kind=idea | scale=esoi/idea-rating-scale.md | min-pass-rate=0.75 | when=a new alternative is described: rate its description on the five questions of the scale before it is built] > offline [real=no | gate=all-pass | when=the registry and tier-selection tests pass] > one [sample=sample:1 | real=yes | gate=all-pass | when=a single real case runs end to end and is hand-read] > staged [sample=sample | real=yes | gate=competitive | max-age-days=90 | when=the tier default is being challenged and the spend is approved]

name: Fast tier default
purpose: The fast tier's default is the cheapest and fastest model that is good enough for short structured calls, by public evaluations, list price and published speed.
record: Form: the cheapest and fastest model that is at least as good as what does the tier's job today. The minimum on each evaluation the tier names is the score of the tier's held default (tier_arms.csv; the anchor, recorded with its model and date in tier_metrics.csv) at its documented default effort, less a 5 percent tolerance for benchmark noise (the evaluations publish no interval in our data); an evaluation on which the anchor has no current number is dropped from the minimums and listed, never guessed. An arm is eligible with a current number on every remaining evaluation, a list price (input plus output USD per million tokens, the price row in force today) and a published output speed; it clears when it reaches every minimum, so the held default always clears its own and a tier never moves to a dearer model merely because a stronger one exists. Among clearing arms score = K^wc x S^ws x (1 + bonus x C), where K is the cheapest clearing arm's price divided by the arm's, S the arm's output speed divided by the fastest clearing arm's, wc + ws = 1, and C (0 to 1) the weighted share of the best value on the evaluations. Nothing is imputed; rows older than 45 days are not used; an arm at an effort other than the model's documented default competes only when its caller applies the effort. Weights, bonus and anchors are in tier_metrics.csv with their reasons. Fast anchor: the held default of the fast tier; factors cost 0.5, speed 0.5; capability bonus at most 10 percent. The result is marked proxy evidence.
disadvantages: This form replaced two earlier ones, both written after rankings were seen: a floor relative to the best eligible arm let the strongest model push the next one out, and hand-set absolute minimums were guesses on benchmark scales we do not own and again chose the top model on a one-provider install (the mid model missed one minimum by 0.04 and 0.01). Raising a tier's bar is a recorded change to its anchor with the solution-level evidence that the tier's work needs more; that is where a solution's own measurements come in. No public evaluation covers classification or extraction on current models, so every fast evaluation is a proxy (marked proxy evidence in the result); speed is output tokens per second and ignores reasoning latency; one aggregator supplies the numbers. The role-tier metric (metric-role-tier, role_tiers.csv) decides which tier a call role uses, not which model the tier maps to.
cascading_conditionals: idea [kind=idea | scale=esoi/idea-rating-scale.md | min-pass-rate=0.75 | when=a new alternative is described: rate its description on the five questions of the scale before it is built] > offline [real=no | gate=all-pass | when=hubofhubs/the_world/model_plumbing/tests/test_tier_public_metric.py passes] > public [real=no | gate=competitive | max-age-days=45 | when=every required public row of the arm is present and no older than 45 days]

name: Fast roles pooled cases
purpose: Whether a tier's model does the jobs of the call roles that resolve to the fast tier (classification, representative selection, folder view picking) as well as the tier above, on those roles' own existing cases pooled into one stage.
record: Pooled pass rate over the cases of the fast roles (request classification, representative selection, folder view picking), each with its source's label; per-role and per-kind rates, hand-offs of a goal a person must keep, tokens and the cost the provider reports. Fixed before scoring: every case counts once; a reply that cannot be read fails; a tier is adequate when its pooled rate is within a 5 percent tolerance of the reference's (evaluation/fast_roles_pool/score.py).

name: Role tier by public evaluations
purpose: The tier a call role uses is the lowest tier unless the next tier up shows a significant gain on the public evaluations that speak to the role's kind of call, with the owner's hard constraints applied after the metric and recorded as such. A deep-run role (deep work, main session, sub-agents) instead uses the cheapest tier that is good enough to get most tasks done by recorded evidence, unless the person names a higher one now or in earlier guidance, or a failed task escalates one rung for a stated reason.
record: Per role: its kind, frequency class and stakes class (role_tiers.csv); per kind the public evaluations with a weight and a direct or proxy mark, one ladder, the base gain, the frequency and stakes factors and the price premium (role_tier_metrics.csv, written 2026-11-11 before any role was computed); the models that fill the tiers from the tier choice and their rows in tier_public_scores.csv and prices in tier_prices.csv. Rule: gain = the weighted share of the better of the two tiers' models that the higher one adds, over the kind's evaluations (an Elo rating read as a chance of beating the better one; an evaluation with no number on both is dropped and listed); the role steps up when gain reaches the larger of the noise floor (0.10) and 3 x the expected added cost / the value of a full gain, where the added cost is calls per turn or run (many 10, turn 2, rare 0.5) x the list price differences times the role's input and output tokens per call (measured where a measurement exists, else an estimated class small, medium or large; deep-work sessions use the measured median of recorded sessions, with cache reads and writes priced at their multipliers of the input price), and the value of a full gain is stated by the stakes class (call 0.05, turn 1, task 10, structure 50 USD); the metric climbs only as far as quality. The form was revised once on the owner's instruction on 2026-11-11 after the first table was seen (his words and the changes are the revision rows of role_tier_metrics.csv). Deep-run roles (the deep_run rows of role_tier_metrics.csv: the four deep-work roles by task kind, main_session, sub_agent, after_check_resume, the solution agents, the structure and foundational task roles, and file editing) do not use that climb. File editing is judged on its own recorded measurement, the component file_edit_goals of esoi/results.csv (the own_evidence rows), under the same bar of 0.66; a run counts only within 90 days and when recorded under the model the tier names on the day of the computation, otherwise that tier is unmeasured and the rule's fallback applies (the previous tier is kept, and the row says why). Their definition, from the owner's instruction of 2026-11-12 (revision 4), is: (1) default = the lowest tier whose measured pass rate on the recorded hard deep-work cases meets the sufficiency bar of 0.66 (stated once in role_tier_metrics.csv; source: the min-pass-rate of the whole stage of metric-delegated-agent-sessions-hard, set before this rule), measured as passed over total of every recorded arm row of the tier in arm_standings.json beside delegated_agent_sessions; a tier with no measurement is skipped, so the default is the cheapest measured tier that meets the bar and the row says so; (2) the person may set higher: the tier named in the current request wins, then the tier a standing-guidance function the consumer supplies names (StandingTierGuidance; the hub holds no preference store), then the default; (3) when the default fails a task (the after-run check, the stop decision or a review says the result is insufficient) the planner may move that task up one rung, never to best, with a specific reason that is recorded with the run as tier_reason (with tier, tier_source and tier_from in the run record), and the next task starts again from (2); (4) a sub-agent runs on its own default whatever the main session runs on, unless the main session asks for a named tier and gives a reason. main_session follows the implementation role when the kind is not known. Hard constraints after the metric, each with its reason in the file: classification fast only, a response a person reads at least balanced, best only for the structure watch (or a person's request), and connected system operations at least quality (an operation on a connected system can have a significant downstream effect if wrong and no measurement of the tiers on such operations exists; a person may set it higher). Each row's evidence names the evaluations, the two tiers' scores, the gap against the threshold, the date, direct or proxy, and the metric alone's pick where a constraint set the tier. Numbers older than the 45 day limit are reported in the row and the previous tier is kept. hubofhubs.the_world.model_plumbing.model_tier_chooser.role_tiers.compute_table recomputes the table; a test pins the file to it.
disadvantages: This metric family was retuned after seeing results three times; the rule was written first and is changed only as a new recorded row with the table recomputed once. No public evaluation measures classification, orchestration or review directly (those kinds rest on proxies); one aggregator supplies every number; the evaluations publish no interval, so the base gain is a choice twice the tier tolerance; the two tiers' models run at different default reasoning efforts and list price ignores reasoning tokens; the frequency and stakes class of each role is read from its call path. Plainly: (1) the added cost uses list prices and the tokens per call of the role, which are measured for some roles (the classification, folder view, card, search, file editing and structure watch roles, from small evaluation cases; the deep-work roles, from the median of 1373 recorded Claude Code sessions of at least 10 assistant messages measured 2026-11-11, with cache writes and reads priced at the registry's multipliers of 1.25 and 0.1 of the input price for the models that carry them, and no discount assumed where a multiplier is blank) and estimated for the rest (small, medium and large classes); the sessions sampled are all kinds of work on one machine, not only the task kinds the roles name, and the median session is used, not the larger ones (the 75th percentile is recorded in role_tier_metrics.csv, not used); list price ignores reasoning tokens; the dollar values of a full gain by stakes class (0.05, 1, 10 and 50 USD) and the cost weight of 3 are ASSUMPTIONS with no recorded source (the owner's tier meanings fix their order, not their size). Since revision 4 these assumptions govern the per-call roles only; no deep-run role depends on them (pinned by a test); (2) the models that fill two tiers run at different default reasoning efforts, so part of a gap between them is effort and one board cannot separate it; (3) several steps sit close to their thresholds (the balanced to quality step of the work kind is a gain of 0.117 against a bound of 0.10 for file editing and connected system operations (noise floor); the critical review step is close to its bound too), so a small change in a score or weight flips the tier and those rows are not strong signals; (4) the non-hallucination evaluation scores the lower tier's model higher than the higher tier's, so the weight a kind gives it decides the gap for gather, orchestrate, write and review kinds, and that weight is a choice made before computing, not a measurement. The earlier forms put deep implementation on quality by a margin of 0.001 under those assumed weights; revision 4 replaced weight balancing for the deep-run roles with the sufficiency rule, whose weaknesses are: only the fast tier has a recorded deep-work measurement (the hard cases of delegated agent sessions on three harnesses; the balanced and quality tiers have none, so the rule cannot say whether they would do better, and escalation is the planner's remedy); the cases are repository tasks, not structure work or review as such, so the same evidence serves every deep-run role; a small case set gives wide intervals around the pass rate that is compared with the bar; the bar is the hub's existing floor for counting an arm, not a derived measure of what most tasks need; passing the cases says nothing of a task's quality beyond the case checks; and the standing-guidance source is a function the consumer must supply, so a consumer that does not supply one gets only the current request and the default.
